lead: The first law of thermodynamics says energy is conserved. For a closed system, the heat added minus the work done equals the change in internal energy stored inside. Over a complete cycle the system returns to its starting state, so the net heat equals the net work. This one balance finds unknown heat, work or internal-energy change in any process, it gives the area inside a p-V loop a meaning, and it rules out any machine that claims to create energy. Every engine, refrigerator and pressure vessel in later units is checked against it first.
prereq: You need: the closed system, state, path, cycle and the sign convention for work and heat from Unit 1 (Foundations); Chapter 2.2 then names the property U properly.

blocks.text: The first law states: when a closed system moves from state 1 to state 2, the heat added to it minus the work done by it equals the change in its internal energy. No mass crosses the boundary of a closed system; energy crosses only as heat and work. Internal energy U is the energy stored in the matter itself, in kJ.

blocks.where: Q₁₂ is the heat added to the system during the process (kJ); W₁₂ is the work done by the system (kJ); U₁ and U₂ are internal energies at the start and end states (kJ); ΔU is their difference (kJ).

blocks.text: The signs are fixed by convention. Heat added to the system is positive, heat rejected is negative. Work done by the system is positive, work done on the system is negative. With that convention one equation covers every case, so you never flip a sign by hand.

blocks.where: δQ and δW are small heat and work transfers in an infinitesimal step, written with δ because they depend on the path; dU is the small change of the property U.

blocks.text: Over a complete cycle the system returns to state 1, so ΔU = 0 and the balance becomes ∮δQ = ∮δW. The symbol ∮ means sum around the whole cycle: net heat in equals net work out. Some syllabi call the process form 'the first law applied to a process'. A control mass means the same thing as a closed system.

sections.h3: Heat and work follow the path; U does not

blocks.text: U depends only on the state, so ΔU between two states is fixed however you travel between them. Q and W are transfers, not stored quantities, so they depend on the route.
Path B does only 10 kJ of work, so it needs 60 kJ of heat to reach the same state. Both paths give ΔU = 50 kJ. You can say 'the internal energy of state 2'; you cannot say 'the heat of state 2'.

items: An isolated system has Q = 0 and W = 0, so ΔU = 0: its energy stays constant.
A cycle that delivers net work must absorb net heat equal to it.
A cycle with net work but zero net heat is impossible. That device is the perpetual motion machine of the first kind, covered in Chapter 2.5.

sections.h3: Work is the area under the process curve

blocks.text: For a quasi-static process the displacement work is the area under the curve on a p-V diagram, taken from Unit 1:

blocks.where: p is absolute pressure (kPa), dV the small volume change (m³), and the integral runs along the actual path from 1 to 2; W comes out in kJ when p is in kPa and V in m³.

blocks.text: Expansion gives dV > 0 and W > 0, work done by the system. Compression gives W < 0. Two different paths between the same states enclose different areas, which is the geometric reason W is path-dependent.

For a cycle the outbound and return curves enclose a loop. The net work is the enclosed area: positive when the loop runs clockwise on the p-V diagram, negative when anticlockwise. That area equals the net heat, exactly as ∮δQ = ∮δW says.

figure.caption: Heat enters the closed system and work leaves it; both are measured at the boundary, while ΔU is the change of the energy stored inside.

spec.title: Energy balance for a closed system
spec.aria: Heat enters a closed system, the internal energy inside changes, and work leaves the system.

examples.question: A gas in a piston-cylinder device receives 80 kJ of heat and does 30 kJ of work as it goes from state 1 to state 2. (a) Find the change in internal energy. (b) The gas is then brought back to state 1 along a path in which 20 kJ of work is done on the gas. Find the heat transfer for the return path. (c) Verify the cycle form of the first law.
steps: Apply the process form to path 1 → 2: Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = U₂ − U₁.
Substitute: 80 kJ − 30 kJ = 50 kJ, so U₂ − U₁ = 50 kJ. The internal energy rises by 50 kJ.
For the return path 2 → 1, the internal-energy change reverses: U₁ − U₂ = −50 kJ.
Work is done on the gas, so W = −20 kJ by the sign convention.
Rearrange to Q = ΔU + W = −50 kJ + (−20 kJ) = −70 kJ. The gas rejects 70 kJ of heat.
Net heat over the cycle: Q_net = 80 − 70 = 10 kJ. Net work over the cycle: W_net = 30 − 20 = 10 kJ.
Q_net = W_net = 10 kJ, so the cycle form ∮δQ = ∮δW is satisfied.
examples.answer: ΔU = +50 kJ for 1 → 2; the return path rejects 70 kJ of heat; over the cycle Q_net = W_net = 10 kJ.
examples.check:
dU = 80 - 30
Q_return = -dU + (-20)
Q_net = 80 + Q_return
W_net = 30 - 20
print(dU)
print(Q_return)
print(Q_net)
print(W_net)

traps: Calling Q or W a property: 'the heat of state 2' is wrong, only U is stored and state-fixed.
Sign slip when work is done on the system: W = −20 kJ, not +20 kJ. Adding it instead of subtracting turns −70 kJ into −30 kJ.
Using Q − W = ΔU for a turbine, nozzle or any open system. Mass carries energy in and out there; use the steady flow energy equation in Chapter 2.6.
Mixing kJ with kJ/kg: if the question gives 80 kJ/kg and the mass is 2 kg, multiply before you add or subtract.
For a cycle, quoting net work without checking net heat, or the reverse. The examiner checks that both come out equal.

quiz.q: State the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system undergoing a process.
quiz.a: The heat added to a closed system minus the work done by it equals the change in its internal energy: Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = U₂ − U₁.

quiz.q: Write the first law for a complete cycle and explain why it takes that form.
quiz.a: ∮δQ = ∮δW. The system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and the balance reduces to net heat = net work.

quiz.q: Why is U called a property but Q is not?
quiz.a: U is fixed by the state, so ΔU between two states is the same along every path. Q is energy in transit across the boundary and its value changes with the path taken, so it belongs to the process, not to the state.

quiz.q: A gas absorbs 120 kJ of heat and its internal energy falls by 40 kJ. Find the work done, with its sign.
quiz.a: Q − W = ΔU, so W = Q − ΔU = 120 − (−40) = 160 kJ. Positive, so 160 kJ of work is done by the gas.

quiz.q: In a cycle, 200 kJ of heat enters and the net work output is 120 kJ. How much heat is rejected?
quiz.a: Cycle form: Q_net = W_net = 120 kJ. Q_net = Q_in − Q_out, so Q_out = 200 − 120 = 80 kJ rejected.

quiz.q: A device claims to deliver 100 kJ of work per cycle while receiving only 60 kJ of heat and rejecting nothing. Which law does it break and why?
quiz.a: It breaks the first law. For a cycle Q_net must equal W_net, so W_net cannot be 100 kJ when Q_net is 60 kJ; the missing 40 kJ would have to be created. It is a perpetual motion machine of the first kind.

quiz.q: A student writes Q + W = ΔU, keeping W positive when done by the system. Show with the cycle form why the convention fails.
quiz.a: Around a cycle ΔU = 0, so the student's equation would give Q_net + W_net = 0, meaning a heat engine that produces work must absorb negative heat. That contradicts ∮δQ = ∮δW, so the sign on W must be reversed to Q − W = ΔU.

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant energy audits, the first law balance is applied to every stream of a boiler or a chiller to find where kJ are leaking away; that bookkeeping is the first step before any exergy analysis in Unit 4. Computational fluid dynamics codes solve the differential form δQ − δW = dU cell by cell, which is why the same equation appears in heat-transfer software. Battery and thermal-storage designers use it to check that the heat measured out of a pack matches the electrical work in. Search 'energy balance closed system', 'first law control mass' and 'p-V diagram cycle work' to go further.
